Administration & Best Practices:
Administration & Best Practices

Use this page to keep Trivy stable, secure, and useful over time. The goal is not just to deploy Trivy once, but to make sure teams continue trusting and using the scan results.

Keep the Vulnerability Database Healthy

  • Ensure the Trivy server can reach the advisory databases or an approved internal mirror
  • Monitor startup logs after deploy and after upgrades to confirm DB download and refresh are working
  • If your network requires a proxy or custom CA bundle, configure that early — DB sync issues are a common cause of stale results

Secure the Service

  • Keep the Trivy service cluster-internal unless there is a clear need for external access
  • If external access is required, put it behind authentication, TLS, and network restrictions
  • Treat registry credentials and proxy credentials as secrets, not plain values in Helm files
  • Give only the required namespace and RBAC access to the teams that operate or validate Trivy

Manage Performance and Resource Usage

  • Server mode is the main optimization for shared environments because it prevents repeated DB downloads
  • Large Java or multi-layer images can take longer to analyze; use a larger timeout where needed
  • Tune CPU, memory, and node placement based on real scan volume rather than guessing upfront
  • Watch PVC health and storage growth if scans are frequent or the environment is long-lived

Set Clear Scan Policy

  • Define what blocks a release: for example HIGH and CRITICAL findings with available fixes
  • Separate gating scans from reporting scans so teams do not ignore everything at once
  • Review ignore rules regularly and give each exception an owner, business reason, and expiry date

Handle Private Registries Correctly

  • Make sure scan clients can authenticate to private registries before rollout day
  • If your registry uses self-signed certificates, distribute the trusted CA instead of defaulting to insecure access
  • Test at least one private image scan during onboarding — this is a frequent integration gap

Upgrade Process

Upgrades should be small and testable. Keep a copy of your working values file, update dependencies, redeploy, and validate with a real scan after the rollout.

helm dependency build .
helm --kubeconfig <kubeconfig-path> --kube-context <context>           upgrade --install trivy .           --namespace <namespace>           -f <values-override.yaml>           --wait           --timeout 10m

Recommended Operating Checklist

  • Weekly: confirm the service is healthy and still serving test scans
  • Weekly: review any repeated scan failures, timeout patterns, or DB sync warnings
  • Monthly: review ignored findings and remove stale exceptions
  • Quarterly: review chart version, Trivy release notes, and network/proxy assumptions

When to Add Trivy Operator

If the customer wants continuous in-cluster security visibility across workloads and Kubernetes resources, Trivy Operator can complement this server-based setup. For many teams, however, starting with Trivy Server plus CI/CD scanning is the simpler first step.

OpenHands Deployment Runbook

This runbook describes the standard approach for deploying OpenHands as a Shakudo-managed stack component in a customer environment. It is intended for public-facing deployment guidance and avoids customer-specific hostnames, secrets, private URLs, and environment names.

Deployment Overview

  • Deployment model: OpenHands runs inside the customer Shakudo cluster as a managed stack component.
  • Primary user entry point: customers launch OpenHands from Shakudo Stack Components after deployment is complete.
  • Shakudo manages platform routing, authentication integration, Kubernetes deployment, and operational validation.
  • Customer-specific values such as domains, namespaces, credentials, storage classes, and Git provider settings should be supplied through the approved deployment configuration.

Prerequisites

  • A running Shakudo customer environment with Kubernetes access for the deployment operator.
  • OpenHands container image and chart or manifest version approved for the target environment.
  • A namespace selected for OpenHands, usually managed with the rest of the Shakudo stack components.
  • Approved secret-management path for API keys, Git credentials, model provider credentials, and integration tokens.
  • Persistent storage class available if the deployment stores sessions, workspace state, or runtime artifacts.

Step 1 — Prepare deployment values

# Set environment-specific values before rendering manifests.
# Replace placeholders with approved customer-environment values.

export OPENHANDS_NAMESPACE="openhands"
export OPENHANDS_RELEASE="openhands"
export OPENHANDS_IMAGE="<approved-openhands-image>:<version>"
export OPENHANDS_HOST="<openhands-subdomain>.<customer-domain>"
export STORAGE_CLASS="<storage-class>"

kubectl create namespace "$OPENHANDS_NAMESPACE" --dry-run=client -o yaml > namespace.yaml

Step 2 — Create required secrets

# Create secrets from the approved secret-management source.
# Do not commit real secret values to Git or public documentation.

kubectl -n "$OPENHANDS_NAMESPACE" create secret generic openhands-secrets   --from-literal=MODEL_API_KEY="<model-provider-api-key>"   --from-literal=GIT_TOKEN="<git-provider-token>"   --dry-run=client -o yaml > openhands-secrets.yaml

# Review the generated manifest and store/apply it through the approved deployment workflow.

Step 3 — Configure Helm values or manifests

# Example values file structure. Adjust names to match the approved chart or manifest package.cat > openhands-values.yaml <<'EOF'
image:
 repository: <approved-openhands-image-repository>
 tag: <version>

service:
 type: ClusterIP
 port: 3000

ingress:
 enabled: true
 host: <openhands-subdomain>.<customer-domain>
 tls: true

persistence:
 enabled: true
 storageClass: <storage-class>
 size: 20Gi

auth:
 mode: shakudo

secrets:
 existingSecret: openhands-secrets

resources:
 requests:
   cpu: "1"
   memory: 2Gi
 limits:
   cpu: "4"
   memory: 8Gi
EOF

Step 4 — Deploy OpenHands

# Apply namespace and secrets through the approved deployment process.
kubectl apply -f namespace.yaml
kubectl apply -f openhands-secrets.yaml

# Deploy with Helm when a chart is used.
helm upgrade --install "$OPENHANDS_RELEASE" <openhands-chart>   --namespace "$OPENHANDS_NAMESPACE"   --values openhands-values.yaml

# Wait for the workload to become ready.
kubectl -n "$OPENHANDS_NAMESPACE" rollout status deploy/openhands --timeout=300s

kubectl -n "$OPENHANDS_NAMESPACE" get svc
kubectl -n "$OPENHANDS_NAMESPACE" get ingress

# Check recent logs for startup or configuration errors.

Commands fail inside the session

  • Check whether dependencies are installed in the selected environment.
  • Confirm the command works for the same repository outside OpenHands if you have terminal access.
  • Ask OpenHands to inspect the error and propose the smallest environment fix before changing code.
  • Escalate recurring environment issues to the Shakudo admin or support path.

OpenHands made a change I do not want

  • Review the diff or changed files before accepting or merging anything.
  • Ask OpenHands to revert the specific change if the session supports edits.
  • Use your source control workflow to discard unwanted changes when needed.
  • Capture the prompt and session summary if you need support to investigate.

How should production changes be handled?

  • Use OpenHands to assist with implementation, investigation, and validation.
  • Keep production-bound changes in the customer’s normal pull request, review, test, and deployment process.
  • Do not bypass required approvals because a change was generated by OpenHands.

What should I include when asking for support?

  • Shakudo workspace and environment.
  • OpenHands component page or session identifier, if available.
  • Time of the issue and the user or role affected.
  • Repository or project context, excluding sensitive secrets.
  • Exact error message, screenshot, or command output.
Administration & Best Practices:
Administration and Best Practices

Administer OpenHands through Shakudo’s workspace, component, and access-control model. Keep customer usage safe by controlling who can launch sessions, what repositories are available, and which credentials or integrations are exposed.

Access management

  • Grant OpenHands access only to users or groups that need AI-assisted engineering workflows.
  • Use least-privilege repository and credential access.
  • Separate development, staging, and production permissions when possible.
  • Review access regularly as teams and projects change.

Session management

  • Encourage users to create task-specific sessions instead of broad, open-ended sessions.
  • Name sessions with the project, task, and date when the UI supports it.
  • Close or archive sessions that are no longer needed according to customer retention policies.
  • Preserve relevant logs and summaries for support or audit review.

Credential and integration practices

  • Expose only the credentials required for the task.
  • Avoid using production secrets for exploratory tasks.
  • Rotate credentials through the customer’s standard process if they may have been exposed to an unintended workspace or session.
  • Document which integrations are approved for OpenHands usage.

Engineering workflow best practices

  • Start with read-only inspection when working in a new repository.
  • Require explicit validation steps for code changes.
  • Keep changes small and reviewable.
  • Use pull requests or the customer’s normal review workflow for any production-bound changes.
  • Do not treat AI-generated output as automatically approved.

Operational monitoring

  • Monitor session failures, permission errors, and repeated environment setup issues.
  • Track common onboarding problems and convert them into templates or runbook updates.
  • Escalate platform-level issues through Shakudo support with workspace, component, session, and timestamp details.
